newsitem.title: UK: Britain launches new "Gulf War syndrome" study.
newsitem.headline: Britain launches new "Gulf War syndrome" study.

text.p: Britain on Tuesday announced a new research programme into the illnesses suffered by veterans of the Gulf War after pressure from ex-servicemen and women.

The three-year study, to be funded by the defence ministry, comes after a government admission that, contrary to what ministers said in the past, so-called organophosphate pesticides had been more widely used in the Gulf than had been thought.
Armed Forces minister Nicholas Soames said the government had "every sympathy" for ill veterans of the 1991 war.
But he added: "We retain an open mind about the question of whether there is or is not a Gulf War syndrome."
The opposition Labour party immediately criticised the government for taking too long to respond to veterans' concerns.

"This represents a victory for those of us who have been campaigning for more openness and more urgency in the government's response to illnesses suffered by people who had served in the Gulf War," said Labour's David Clark.

Veterans also expressed frustration that the government had taken so long to agree to a full study, which will check whether Gulf veterans have more illnesses than those who did not serve in the area and whether their children are affected.
Tony Flint, a leader of a veterans organisation who suffers from a range of symptoms, said: "Too little, too late. ... The damage has already been done."
Flint said there would be a three year wait for the results of the survey, during which veterans would continue to die.

The government's admission it gave misleading information to parliament on the use of pesticides and its decision to go ahead with the major new study -- which will cost 1.3 million pounds ($2.15 million) -- was a significant shift of position.
The government has insisted there is no single syndrome to explain the illnesses of the Gulf War veterans.
But lawyers for more than 1,000 British veterans who say they are suffering from Gulf War syndrome said last month they they would issue writs against the defence ministry in January.

The veterans say evidence collected in the United States supports their argument that there is in fact a syndrome caused by a "cocktail" of immunisations to protect them against chemical and biological warfare and by the pesticides.
About 51,000 Britons were involved in the war against Iraq following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.

Around 750 veterans have complained of chronic fatigue, asthma, depression and skin complaints. Some are now confined to wheelchairs and say their children have suffered birth defects. ($1=.6047 Pound)
